title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: Kutuzov's order to retreat through Moscow to the Ryazan road was issued on the night of September 1.

The first troops set out at once, marching slowly and steadily through the night without haste. At daybreak, however, those approaching the city at the Dorogomilov bridge found masses of soldiers crowding and rushing across the bridge ahead of them, jamming the streets and alleys on the far side, while endless columns bore down from behind. An unreasoning panic and urgency overcame them all. They surged forward to the bridge, onto it, and toward the fords and boats. Kutuzov himself had taken a detour through side streets to the other side of Moscow.
By ten in the morning of September 2, only the rear guard remained in the Dorogomilov district, with plenty of room. The main army was on the other side of Moscow or already beyond it.

At that very hour — ten in the morning of September 2 — Napoleon was standing among his troops on Poklonny Hill, surveying the panorama spread before him. From August 26 to September 2 — from the Battle of Borodino to the French entry into Moscow — during that whole stirring, memorable week, there had been the kind of extraordinary autumn weather that always comes as a surprise: when the sun hangs low and gives more warmth than in spring, when everything shines so brightly in the rare clear air that it stings the eyes, when the lungs feel strengthened and refreshed by the fragrant autumn air, when even the nights are warm, and when from those dark warm skies golden stars constantly startle and delight by falling.
At ten on the morning of September 2, this weather still held.

The brightness of the morning was magical. Moscow, seen from Poklonny Hill, lay spaciously spread out with its river, gardens, and churches, and seemed to be living its usual life, its domes glittering like stars in the sunlight.

The view of the strange city with its unfamiliar architecture filled Napoleon with the rather envious and uneasy curiosity men feel when encountering a foreign way of life that knows nothing of them. This city was clearly alive with the full force of its own existence. By those indefinable signs that even at a distance distinguish a living body from a dead one, Napoleon sensed from Poklonny Hill the throb of life in the city and felt, as it were, the breathing of that great and beautiful body.

Every Russian looking at Moscow feels her to be a mother; every foreigner who sees her, even without knowing her significance as the mother city, must sense her feminine character. And Napoleon felt it.

"That Asian city of countless churches — holy Moscow! Here it is at last, that famous city. It was high time," he said, and dismounting, he ordered a map of Moscow spread before him and summoned his interpreter, Lelorgne d'Ideville.
* "That Asian city of countless churches — holy Moscow! Here it is at last, that famous city. It was high time."

"A town captured by the enemy is like a maiden who has lost her honor," he thought (he had said as much to Tuchkov at Smolensk). From that vantage point he gazed at the Eastern beauty he hadn't seen before. It seemed strange that his long-held wish, which had seemed unattainable, was at last realized. In the clear morning light he looked from the city to the map and back again, and the certainty of possessing it both excited and awed him.

"But could it have been otherwise?" he thought. "Here is this capital at my feet. Where is Alexander now, and what is he thinking? A strange, beautiful, majestic city — and a strange and majestic moment! In what light must I appear to them!" he reflected, thinking of his troops. "Here she is — the reward for all those fainthearted men," he mused, glancing at his entourage and the approaching troops. "One word from me, one movement of my hand, and that ancient capital of the Tsars would perish. But my clemency is always ready to descend upon the vanquished. I must be magnanimous and truly great. But no — it can't be true that I'm in Moscow," he suddenly thought. "Yet here she lies at my feet, with her golden domes and crosses gleaming in the sun. But I shall spare her. On the ancient monuments of barbarism and despotism I shall inscribe great words of justice and mercy. This is what Alexander will feel most keenly — I know him." (It seemed to Napoleon that the chief significance of events lay in his personal rivalry with Alexander.) "From the heights of the Kremlin — yes, there it is — I shall give them just laws. I shall teach them what true civilization means. I shall make generations of boyars remember their conqueror with love. I shall tell the delegation that I did not and do not wish for war, that I have fought only against the false policy of their court; that I love and respect Alexander and that in Moscow I shall accept peace terms worthy of myself and my peoples. 'Boyars,' I shall say to them, 'I do not desire war. I desire the peace and welfare of all my subjects.' However, I know their presence will inspire me, and I shall speak as I always do — clearly, impressively, and majestically. But can it really be true that I'm in Moscow? Yes, there she lies."
"Bring the boyars to me," he said to his entourage.
* "Bring the boyars to me."
A general with a brilliant retinue galloped off at once to fetch the boyars.

Two hours passed. Napoleon had lunched and was standing again in the same spot on Poklonny Hill, waiting for the delegation. His speech to the boyars had already taken definite shape in his imagination. That speech was full of dignity and grandeur as Napoleon understood them.

He was carried away by the tone of magnanimity he planned to adopt toward Moscow. In his mind he set dates for assemblies at the Tsar's palace where Russian dignitaries and his own people would mingle. He mentally appointed a governor, one who would win the people's hearts. Knowing there were many charitable institutions in Moscow, he decided he would shower them all with favors. He thought that just as in Africa he had worn a burnoose and sat in a mosque, so in Moscow he must be beneficent like the Tsars. And to touch the hearts of the Russians — and being, like all Frenchmen, unable to imagine anything sentimental without a reference to his dear, tender, poor mother — he decided to place an inscription on every institution: "Dedicated to my dear mother." Or no, simply: "House of My Mother," he concluded. "But am I really in Moscow? Yes, here it lies before me — but why is the city delegation taking so long?" he wondered.
* "My dear, my tender, my poor mother."
* "House of My Mother."

Meanwhile, at the rear of his retinue, an anxious consultation was being conducted in whispers among his generals and marshals. Those sent to bring the delegation had returned with the news that Moscow was empty — everyone had left. The faces of those not whispering together were pale and worried. They were not alarmed by the fact that Moscow had been abandoned (grave as that was), but by the question of how to tell the Emperor — without putting him in the terrible position of looking ridiculous — that he had been waiting for the boyars in vain, that there were only drunken mobs left in Moscow and no one else. Some said a delegation of some kind had to be scraped together; others argued that the Emperor should first be carefully and skillfully prepared, then told the truth.
"He'll have to be told, all the same," said some of the staff. "But, gentlemen..."

The situation was all the more awkward because the Emperor, meditating on his magnanimous plans, was pacing patiently before the spread-out map, occasionally shading his eyes to look down the road to Moscow with a bright, proud smile.
"But it's impossible..." muttered the staff members, shrugging their shoulders but not daring to say the implied word — ridiculous.

At last the Emperor, tired of waiting — his actor's instinct telling him that the sublime moment, having been drawn out too long, was beginning to lose its sublimity — gave a sign with his hand. A single signal gun was fired, and the troops spread out around Moscow streamed into the city through the Tver, Kaluga, and Dorogomilov gates. Faster and faster, racing each other, they moved at double time or at a trot, vanishing in clouds of dust and making the air ring with a deafening roar of mingled shouts.

Drawn on by the movement of his troops, Napoleon rode with them as far as the Dorogomilov gate, but there he stopped again, dismounted, and paced for a long time by the Kammer-Kollezhsky rampart, waiting for the delegation.
